articles.title: These bookshops let Chinese readers question their country - now the doors are closing
articles.summary: For some mainlanders, Hong Kong's independent bookstores are a window into a different, freer world.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
The owner of Hunter bookstore, pictured here, was arrested in late June By Abel U BBC Chinese ,  Reporting from Hong Kong 
- Published 21 August 2026 
When Chen Zhu heads to Hong Kong from mainland China every month, there's one place she always goes: Hunter Bookstore. 
Founded four years ago by a former councillor, the independent bookshop has earned a reputation for stocking what authorities would consider sensitive books - from accounts of Hong Kong's pro-democracy campaigners, to famous allegories on authoritarianism, such as George Orwell's Animal Farm or Hajime Isayama's Manga series Attack on Titan. 
It's a short journey from Zhu's home in Guangzhou on China's southern coast to the crowded street in Hong Kong's Sham Shui Po district, where Hunter is sandwiched between fabric sellers, garages and trendy cafes. 
But, for the 23-year-old, it is also a passage into a different, freer world - where she can find answers to forbidden questions. 
When she learned the bookshop had been raided by police in late June, Zhu broke into tears: "I was devastated." 
Hong Kong saw a boom in independent bookshops after huge pro-democracy protests rocked the city in 2019. But it has been increasingly difficult for them to survive as China's control over the city has grown. 
While Beijing defends its far-reaching National Security Law (NSL) as essential for stability, many Hong Kongers and rights groups argue it has crushed free speech. Thousands of locals, including activists and former lawmakers, have left in recent years, as tough new security laws have led to a slew of arrests and convictions. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Books about the Tiananmen Square democracy movement and billionaire businessman and newspaper founder Jimmy Lai 
When police searched Hunter Bookstore on 24 June, they accused owner Letitia Wong, 33, and a 32-year-old man, of violating those laws and arrested them for sedition and money laundering. They deny the charges and have since been released on bail. 
In March, they arrested the owner of Book Punch, along with three employees on the same charges, and reportedly seized copies of a biography on Jimmy Lai, the jailed democracy campaigner. 
On 15 July, when the annual Hong Kong Book Fair opened, national security police searched two more independent bookshops, Greenfield Bookstore and Have a Nice Stay, arresting five people for sedition. They, too, have been released on bail. 
At the end of the month Greenfield posted on social media, saying: "Our store will be closing after our lease expires. Thank you for walking with us, through wind and rain, for 50 years since our opening." It was the third independent bookshop to shut within a month. 
These bookshops have long had a loyal following not just in Hong Kong, but also among many mainland Chinese readers. Some like Zhu travel to the city in search of a single book. 
For 19-year-old Li from Shanghai, who didn't give her first name, these are places where she "can see so many possibilities, and where existing ideas can be challenged". Others treasure them as spaces that offer a sense of freedom and community they feel is missing on the mainland. 
Now they fear China is eroding that spirit in Hong Kong too. 
Image source, Getty Image caption, 
Police escort a worker out of Have a Nice Stay bookstore, whose t-shirt reads 'I am a bookshop employee' 
When Zhu began university in 2021, she became increasingly curious about lesser-discussed chapters of Chinese history - such as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre, a taboo topic that has been scrubbed off the country's tightly controlled internet. 
The massive student-led protests ended in a bloody army crackdown whose toll is still contested. Beijing said at the time that 200 civilians died, but according to de-classified UK diplomatic cables, at least 10,000 people were killed. 
Zhu sought out films which touch on the era-defining event, but neither epic romance Summer Palace nor the secretly filmed gay drama Lan Yu could satisfy her curiosity. 
She became set on tracking down The Unburned Book by Taiwanese poet Yang Du, a bittersweet reflection on protesters who later went into exile. 
In 2023, as soon as the China-Hong Kong border reopened after the pandemic she made her way to Hong Kong to find it. 
This was when the city's independent bookshops were taking off. People were sharing walking routes online, complete with neighbourhood guides and curated recommendations. 
In bustling Mong Kok there was Luck Win, known for its generous discounts, and Greenfield, with its packed floor-to-ceiling shelves. A short walk away were the cosy Have a Nice Stay, founded by former journalists, which held popular late-night reading sessions, and Elmbook, whose cramped but beloved shelves made regulars feel like they were on a treasure hunt. 
Then there was Book Punch on trendy Tai Nan Street, with a collection as defiant as its motto, "one punch to wake the reader", and the food lovers' favourite, Word by Word in historic Wan Chai, and, of course, Hunter, with a sofa outside where passers-by can take a break. 
That's where Zhu found The Unburned Book. She had tried - and failed - in other stores, so she was surprised when she finally spotted it. 
Hong Kong, once a refuge for those fleeing China post 1989, commemorated the killings every year with a vigil. They gradually disappeared as the new laws targeted political gatherings. 
Still, when Chris, 20, whose name we have changed, travelled to Hong Kong in early June, he found that one bookstore was displaying relevant books, white candles and rolls of masking tape printed with the Roman numerals "VI-IV" - 6-4, a coded way of representing the 4 June anniversary. 
These young people may not be from Hong Kong, but they describe feeling a deep sense of belonging in these bookshops: politically vibrant spaces that engage with the history their governments would rather they forget. 
But it's more than just about the books. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The shuttered entrance to Greenfield Bookstore following the police raid 
Li visited Hong Kong during the Lunar New Year earlier this year, months after a massive apartment blaze in the north-eastern Tai Po district claimed 168 lives. 
At Hunter Bookstore, she discovered a wall covered in black sticky notes, where visitors had left messages of encouragement for those affected by the tragedy. 
Li says this sense of community is difficult to find in mainland China. She says while they have message boards there too, they wouldn't be focused on solidarity with victims of one particular incident, perhaps because authorities are wary of any outpouring of public sentiment. "People can only express themselves indirectly," Li says. 
She was equally struck by another small detail: handwritten notes left by staff alongside the books. Using sticky notes, booksellers had shared reflections on books they had read or highlighted passages they found particularly meaningful. It's not something she had ever seen back home. 
Zhu experiences something similar. "We all love books. We all value independent bookshops. That's why we choose to buy books here." 
She rarely speaks to strangers while browsing, but she never feels like an outsider. The books and events the shops host give her the feeling she's escaped to somewhere with "at least a little freedom of expression". 
"You've left mainland China behind. Of course, you know [this] freedom has its limits. But it's still better than not being able to say anything at all." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hong Kong has lost many independent bookshops over the years - regulars gathered at Mount Zero on its last day in March 2024 
But now Zhu can sense this freedom being curtailed. 
She says she finds herself encountering authorities more often in Hong Kong than in mainland China. At one bookshop event, she recalls government officials entering the premises. "They just sat there listening alongside us." 
Increasing raids have not only targeted explicitly political shops, according to a bookseller who asked not to be identified because of possible repercussions. 
"Luck Win Bookstore and Elmbook have always kept a very low profile," the bookseller says. 
"They rarely make public statements or organise events. I genuinely can't think of anything they could have done to offend the government." 
In the weeks leading up to this year's book fair, both shops were criticised in Wen Wei Po, a newspaper controlled by Beijing's liaison authorities in Hong Kong. 
The paper accused them of selling books promoting "soft resistance". This included The Hong Kong Diaries by the last governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten, before the city returned to Chinese rule, and 300 Short Essays by late Apple Daily columnist Lee Yee. The newspaper was shuttered and several senior staff, including its owner Jimmy Lai, were jailed for violating the new security laws. 
"The authorities don't want people to know exactly where the boundaries are," says Tong Kin-long of University College London. "They want people to work out the red lines for themselves, or to censor themselves before crossing them." 
Watching these changes unfold in Hong Kong has felt strangely familiar to a man we are calling K, in his 30s from Sichuan. 
He remembers a time when mainland China's bookshops were also vibrant spaces for public discussion. Liberal books and magazines would be prominently displayed. Bookshops regularly hosted talks and discussions. But around 2015, he began to notice a gradual tightening. 
At first it was books about the country's leaders. But then less obviously sensitive books started disappearing. Public events became less frequent, and the atmosphere changed. 
Zhu has a friend who currently runs a bookshop in Guangzhou. She says police occasionally visit the shop to harass the bookseller. During film screenings organised by the bookshop, the electricity has even been cut off. 
"Hong Kong," she says, "should be a freer place". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Books by Chinese leader Xi Jinping displayed during the Hong Kong Book Fair in July 
Still, mainland Chinese readers are keen on bringing books home from Hong Kong, even though customs authorities can confiscate those they deem harmful to national sovereignty, security or unity. 
K feels anxious every time he returns from Hong Kong. He chooses busier border crossings, avoids books prominently featuring politically sensitive figures and has hidden books inside his clothes, or deep in his luggage. 
But that is no longer his only worry. "In the past, people would simply think, 'If I can't buy a book in mainland China, I'll go to Hong Kong'. Now the feeling is different. You don't even know which bookshops will still be here the next time you come." 
A week after learning it had been excluded from the Hong Kong Book Fair, Elmbook announced it would close its physical shop in April next year. Soon afterwards, Have A Nice Stay said it would close at the end of August, citing economic difficulties and unpredictable "red lines" over what material was considered problematic. 
Many within Hong Kong's bookselling industry have grown pessimistic. Some believe things will only get worse before they get better. 
But readers are not powerless, an industry insider says. "We can still buy books. We can still read. And we can still read a great many books." 
Chris was frightened after hearing about the arrests at Hunter Bookstore, but he says he will keep going. 
"Buying a book has become a quiet way of showing support, and a quiet form of resistance."

articles.title: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists convicted in national security trial
articles.summary: Three activists were accused of inciting others to subvert state power under the China-introduced law.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Chow Hang-tung had also seperately been arrested in June 2021 for "inciting" the public to take part in a Tiananmen vigil By BBC Chinese 
- Published 21 August 2026 
Two Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown have been found guilty of inciting others to subvert state power under the city's controversial national security law. 
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison after being convicted under the China-introduced law. Sentencing is expected at a later date. 
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty in January. 
Lee and Chow "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power", according to a summary on Friday. Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial. 
Hong Kong used to be one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could gather to mark the deadly 1989 crackdown against pro-democracy protesters. 
Authorities banned these gatherings in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but they have never resumed. This was also the year the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force. 
In mainland China, authorities have banned even oblique references to the 1989 crackdown. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Thousands of people take part in a candlelight vigil at Victoria Park in Hong Kong to mark the 30th anniversary of Beijing's Tiananmen Square crackdown in 1989 
In the courtroom, Chow smiled as the verdict was read out, while Lee showed little emotion as he made a heart gesture and folded his hands to show his gratitude to those in the gallery. 
Lee, a lawmaker, and Chow, a lawyer, were also leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance (HKA), which has been described as a "toxic tumour" by Chinese authorities. 
The HKA was founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies. Weeks later, the Communist Party crushed pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square with troops and tanks. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands. 
Over the next three decades, HKA called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform. 
The Alliance's leaders were charged in 2021 and have been behind bars since. 
Rights group Amnesty International has said the case "relies on vague, overly broad and arbitrary definitions of 'subversion'". 
Sarah Brooks, Amnesty International's deputy regional director, said Chow and Lee had "not committed any recognisable crime". 
"Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan are prisoners of conscience who should never have been prosecuted in the first place. They must be released immediately and unconditionally," she added. 
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the convictions showed "how public displays of mourning have become a crime in Hong Kong". 
In a separate case, Chow was arrested in June 2021 for "inciting" the public to take part in that year's vigil and later found guilty. 
However, Hong Kong's top court overturned that conviction in 2022 , with a judge ruling the police hadn't properly justified the vigil's ban. 
Chow Hang-tung spoke to the BBC in 2021, weeks before her arrest on 4 June 2022. 
"I am prepared to be arrested. That is how Hong Kong is now," she had said. 
"I am willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy." 
Figure caption, 
Lighting a candle for Tiananmen and Hong Kong freedoms 
Critics say the national security law has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear. Authorities insist it is needed to maintain stability. 
Among other things, the law criminalises anything considered as secession - or breaking away from China - as well as subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign or external forces.

articles.title: New Zealand to introduce bill for under-16s social media ban
articles.summary: The government faces opposition to its proposals from MPs who believe a ban will not work.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The proposed ban would apply to platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok By Amy Walker 
- Published 24 August 2026, 13:17 BST 
New Zealand is to introduce a bill seeking to ban under-16s from using social media. 
Under the latest proposals, platforms including TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook, will have to take steps to check users are over 16 and platforms that fail to meet their obligations could face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue. 
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media was exposing children to "harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with". But several political parties have said they will vote against the bill. 
The move follows a similar ban in Australia, while countries including the UK and Greece are set to introduce restrictions next year. 
Luxon said social media was affecting children's family life, mental health, sleep and education. 
"We have protections to keep children safe in the real world and we need them in the virtual world too," he said. 
New Zealand's government has not outlined which other "high risk" platforms could be impacted. 
A statement said that under the Online Safety Bill, which is being introduced to parliament on Monday, social media companies would be required to "take reasonable steps" to check users are over the age of 16 by using methods including existing account information, facial age estimation and digital identity checks. 
Platforms regularly used by children would also be required to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how they are being identified and reduced. 
No penalties are proposed for children, parents or caregivers for breaches of the ban, but fines for social media companies could be substantially higher than in Australia, where the maximum penalty is $99m (£51.7m) .

It is unclear if the bill will get enough votes to pass however, after both the Act and New Zealand First (NZF) parties - which are coalition partners in the government - said they would oppose it. 
David Seymour, New Zealand's deputy prime minister and leader of Act, said the ban would not work. 
Foreign affairs minister Winston Peters, who leads the NZF party, said: "We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country." 
Peters also described a ban introduced in Australia in December as a "colossal failure". 
The ban has been difficult for Australia to enforce, and it has been widely acknowledged that many children under the age of 16 have still been able to access and use banned apps. 
Earlier this month, France's top court struck down a similar proposed social media ban, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression.

articles.title: China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
articles.summary: Using the carcinogen to preserve food is prohibited in China, the world's largest producer of cabbages.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China is the world's largest producer of cabbages By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 24 August 2026, 06:40 BST 
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption. 
Officials in the north-eastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation. 
An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical used for preserving biological specimens that is known to cause cancer, for keeping food fresh is strictly prohibited in China. 
China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia. 
Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media. 
Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country. 
Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables. 
Local authorities in Kangbao county said in a statement issued on Saturday: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply." 
Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market. 
The incident has generated widespread media attention in China. 
An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line." 
China produces well over 30 million tonnes of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable. 
Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles
articles.summary: Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 24 August 2026, 04:27 BST Updated 06:01 BST 
Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles. 
The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations. 
Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely. 
The recalled vehicles will have a warning label stuck on the interior door and receive a software update to automatically lower the windows in a crash. 
The designs have come under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened. 
Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are "difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim". 
"In extreme situations such as a severe collision causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, this could hinder occupants from quickly opening the doors to escape and impede rescue efforts by those outside the vehicle, posing a safety hazard," it said. 
Tesla said it would place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle's windows after a collision. 
It is not clear if the affected firms plan to make a similar recall for the rest of the world. 
The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment. 
The use of hidden handle designs has "snowballed" after Chinese brands were quick to copy the "sleek" look of Tesla's Model S sedan since 2014, said Tu Le, the founder of consultancy Sino Auto Insights. 
The use of warning labels and a software update is more of a "band-aid" than a lasting solution for the issue, he added. 
In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles . 
Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors. 
Tesla's door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars. 
In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers. 
The BBC has contacted the agency for comment.

articles.title: Shein aims for almost $27bn valuation in stock market debut
articles.summary: The fast-fashion giant's shares are due to start trading in Hong Kong on 1 September.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 24 August 2026, 02:23 BST Updated 08:00 BST 
Fast-fashion giant Shein could see its stock market valuation reach almost $27bn (£19.8bn) when its makes its debut in Hong Kong on 1 September. 
The long-awaited move comes after failed attempts to list in the US and London due to regulatory challenges amid scrutiny of the firm, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China. 
Since it was founded in 2008, Shein has risen to become one of the world's biggest fast-fashion retailers, with customers in more than 150 countries. 
The e-commerce giant is known for selling ultra-cheap clothes, backed by a vast network of factories in China that are able to quickly manufacture new products based on the latest trends. 
Shein said in a filing on Monday , external that it will offer nearly 280 million shares for between HK$47.60 ($6.07; £4.45) and HK$49.50 each. 
At the top of the range, the share sale would raise $1.77bn (£1.3bn) for the company and give it a market valuation of $26.8bn. 
But that is much lower than the $100bn it was worth in 2022, reflecting weaker sales growth and higher costs. 
The initial public offering (IPO) is being backed by Wall Street investment giants Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan. 
The company will make its highly anticipated debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after efforts to go public since 2023. 
Hong Kong has been revived as "one of the largest IPO markets" after attracting more firms from mainland China, said economics associate professor Feng Qu from the Nanyang Technological University. 
Shein is likely to command a higher valuation in Hong Kong than it would in London, where regulatory scrutiny derailed its plans to sell shares there, Feng said. 
Chinese companies may also be wary of selling shares in the US as tensions between the world's two largest economies could result in firms being de-listed, he added. 
Competition and roadblocks 
Shein's listing will test investor confidence in the fast-fashion industry and its position in an increasingly competitive market. 
In July, Shein said it had swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty waiver on small packages called the de minimis exemption. 
The company said it lost $99m in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier. 
It also came as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused. 
"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said at the time.

The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets. 
The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing. 
Some investors are questioning whether higher costs and regulatory challenges will affect Shein's ability to get goods swiftly and cheaply to market. 
Marguerite LeRolland from market research company Euromonitor International told the BBC that the firm's sales have slowed in the US partly due to the end of the de minimis exemption . 
The exemption helped retailers like Shein and its fierce rival Temu grow quickly in the US as they were able to deliver goods without incurring import taxes. 
These factors could "narrow the price gap" between Shein and competitors like Primark and H&M, she added. 
Jane Foley, Rabobank's head of FX strategy, told the BBC's Today programme that the ending of the de minimis exemption "really did undermine the core business model of Shein", adding that the EU has done something similar. 
Richard Lim of research firm Retail Economics said Chinese retail giants such as Shein have caused "a huge wave of destruction" in markets like the UK, with more established companies struggling to compete. 
The British retail industry believes Shein is "not playing on a level playing field", he told the BBC. 
It is expected that the UK will impose similar restrictions as the US and EU on small packages from Chinese retailers in 2028. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Shein's fast-fashion clothes are backed by a network of factories in China 
As of the end of March 2026, Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders. 
But its fast-fashion business has faced concerns over its environmental impact, and allegations of forced labour in supply chains. The company has previously told the BBC it has a "zero tolerance for forced labour". 
Its attempt to go public on the London Stock Exchange collapsed after the company came under scrutiny over its refusal to answer questions about its supply chain practices .

articles.title: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US treasury secretary
articles.summary: Scott Bessent says the US will sever all economic ties with the country and that any nation partnering with Iran financially will also be isolated.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Michael Race ,  Reporting from New York   and   Mitchell Labiak ,  Reporting from Business reporters 
- Published 24 August 2026, 11:39 BST Updated 3 hours ago 
The US announced a host of sanctions against Iran and threatened its supporters in what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said was "the single greatest financial offensive ever". 
Labelling it an "economic D-Day" for Iran, Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country and added that any nation financially partnering with Iran would also be isolated. 
However, the latest threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from the White House in its efforts to end the conflict. 
The war has led to hikes in global oil prices, and in response to the latest threat Iran warned it would shut down all oil exports from the region if the war continued. 
The Iranian regime has also issued a fresh warning to shipping to not pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, according to Reuters. 
One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through strait, a narrow waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February, leading to higher oil prices globally. 
At a press conference on Monday outlining what has been called "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the US was launching an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". 
"Iran now faces a very clear choice with only two paths before them: complete global isolation....or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," he said. 
The treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it". 
Bessent said the Treasury Department had mapped networks, facilitators and financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil. 
The department said it has issued determinations against five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels. 
Bessent said that such actions would "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue" for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the wider Iranian regime. 
In a warning to governments and entities assisting or trading with Iran, he said they could not "claim they are blind to enabling this activity". 
He declined to highlight specific countries, but said Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific request to cease their interactions with the regime." 
While he said it was important to give people time to understand the new sanctions, he added: "they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious." 
'Damp squib' 
David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, cast doubt on the effectiveness of the sanctions announcement. 
"With the renewed US naval blockade already strangling Iran's oil exports, the direct impact of 'economic D-Day' on Iran's energy revenues will be somewhat of a damp squib," he said. 
"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term." 
He said that was partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, a country "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either". 
Over the course of the conflict so far, previous threats have included Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz. 
The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy. 
The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel prices much higher than they were a year ago. 
In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November. 
On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $92. 
Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates. 
But the impact of the announcenment was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later.

The Iranian regime already faces tough economic sanctions from the US. 
Former US president Barack Obama and several US allies had agreed a deal with the country in 2015 which lifted many sanctions in return for Iran agreeing to limit its nuclear programme. 
However, Trump pulled out of that deal in 2018, calling it "defective at its core, and reimposed all US sanctions on Iran. 
During Joe Biden's term as US president, he made some attempts to reinstate the Obama-era deal , but this did not happen. 
In April this year, the Trump administration launched a wave of sanctions on foreign banks and firms doing business with Tehran after it became clear its military operations had not caused Iran's regime to surrender.

Watch: Moment humanoid robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m record 
Close 
A robot has outperformed humans by running faster than Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record at the World Humanoid Robot Games in China. 
The humanoid robot, developed by the Beijing Innovation Centre of Humanoid Robotics, ran the distance in 9.39 seconds at the event. 
Eight-time Olympic gold medallist Bolt set the world record for humans in 2009, running 100m in 9.58 seconds. 
The robot beat two others including one made by Chinese smartphone maker Honor - which the manufacturer says ran the distance in 9.32 seconds in a test run. 
Other events at the robot games, which started on Saturday, include boxing and football, but also household tasks such as folding laundry.

Two activists who organised commemorations of the bloody crackdown on China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests now face jail. Remembering is not a crime 
F or decades, Hong Kong mourned when the mainland could not. Its huge annual Tiananmen vigil kept alive the memory of the 1989 pro-reform protests in Beijing, and of the massacre that suppressed them. Along with Macau, it was the only place in China where the anniversary could be publicly marked and the truth preserved. 
But the crackdown on the 2019 uprising in Hong Kong has crushed the freedoms that the region once enjoyed. That year’s vigil was the last. On Friday, two leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which organised the commemoration, were convicted of incitement to subversion under the draconian national security law. Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face up to 10 years in jail. 
A third defendant, the 74-year-old former legislator Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. All three have been imprisoned since their arrests in 2021. The court ruled that the alliance’s stated aim to “end one-party dictatorship” in itself constituted using unlawful means to overthrow the Chinese government – despite acknowledging that the group never used or advocated violence, or even set out a path to its goal. 
The convictions are shameful, but not surprising. They follow the jailing of the prominent pro-democracy activists known as the “ Hong Kong 47 ” in late 2024 and the 20-year sentence handed to the media tycoon and activist Jimmy Lai in February . Yet while this trial shows the authorities’ determination to eradicate Hong Kong’s previous freedoms, it also reflects the Communist party’s determination to control and rewrite history across China . 
View image in fullscreen 
Chow Hang-tung. Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty Images 
Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of people were killed in the 1989 massacre. Xi Jinping made a rare reference to the events last week, reaffirming the party’s “correct” response, in a speech paying tribute to the former leader Jiang Zemin. But the subject remains one of the most taboo in a country long adept at erasing uncomfortable truths – so sensitive that even words such as “remember” and “today” are censored on social media on the anniversary. This June, the Tiananmen Mothers group of bereaved relatives, who have long mourned under heavy police escort , were barred from visiting their loved ones’ graves on the date of the killings. 
Against such brutal edicts, memory appears fragile. Most younger people on the mainland have no idea of what happened. Yet late last year, previously unseen footage suddenly emerged of the court martial of a general who defied the order to use force against demonstrators. The video was posted on YouTube – which is blocked in China – and sheds new light on events. General Xu Qinxian, who was jailed and lived under heavy restrictions until his death in 2021, said that a commander imposing the order might become “a sinner in history”. Whoever leaked the footage, and whatever their reasons for doing so, it is clear that some still resist the national amnesia. 
Remembrance and mourning are not crimes. In a message to Andy Burnham, Ms Chow, a barrister who studied law in the UK, warned that Britain had a “non-delegable duty to adopt a more robust stance” to China. She was right. The UK was the other signatory of the treaty that supposedly preserved Hong Kong’s relative autonomy until 2047. For years in the annual vigils, Ms Chow, Mr Lee and other courageous Hong Kong people stood up for those on the mainland who had been silenced. Others should now stand up and speak for them as they pay the price for that solidarity.

articles.title: Women Photograph announces 2026 grant recipients – in pictures
articles.summary: Women Photograph, a non-profit launched in 2017 to amplify the voices of women and non-binary visual journalists, has announced three recipients of its 2026 grants. Grants of $10,000 have been awarded to Fatma Fahmy, Caroline Gutman and Yixi Tian. This year’s grants were sponsored by Leica USA Continue reading...
articles.full_text:

View image in fullscreen E Ma Huang is a roadside plant commonly encountered when gathering medicinal herbs and is itself a medicine. Yixi Tian’s Veiled by Cloud and Mist follows Miao medicine practitioners, who remain an essential source of care in the mountainous villages of Qiandongnan, Guizhou, China. Guided by her mother, who has long practised among these healers, Yixi Tian has spent years living, learning and documenting alongside them Photograph: Yixi Tian/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Luo Hualü’s van, used for gathering medicinal herbs in the mountains. Through her photographs and the healers’ own words, Yixi Tian captures a world where healing relies on intimate trust and a shared bond with the environment Photograph: TYX/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Yixi Tian has come to see the crises quietly threatening the Miao medicine practitioners’ way of life, including the disappearance of wild herbs, a break in generational transmission and the ongoing limits of formal licensing. Her work stays with those who carry this knowledge as they continue to practice, adapt and hold their world together Photograph: womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Fatma Fahmy’s When Absence Takes Hold is a long-term visual project that explores how the environmental degradation of Lake Qarun in Egypt has reshaped the lives of women in nearby fishing communities. After the construction of Egypt’s High Dam severed the lake’s connection to the Nile, rising salinity, untreated sewage, agricultural runoff, and climate change further transformed the water, causing fish populations to disappear and the shoreline to recede Photograph: Fatma Fahmy/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen ‘Zhiming Pan, 77, is my mother’s herbal medicine teacher and a Miao doctor in Kaili. He continues to see patients from across the region.’ Yixi Tian’s Veiled by Cloud and Mist captures a world where healing relies on intimate trust and a shared bond with the environment. Her work stays with those who carry this knowledge as they continue to practice, adapt and hold their world together Photograph: TYX/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Caroline Gutman’s The Invisible Force is an ongoing documentary project that explores the mystique of nuclear fission and its long-term environmental and social consequences. This chapter focuses on the nuclear mythology surrounding Richland, Washington, which housed workers during the Manhattan Project. Hanford provided plutonium used in the US atomic bomb that killed about thousands of people in Nagasaki in 1945 Photograph: Caroline Gutman/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Darabala Abdel Hadi, 61, fixes his fishing nets in his house in Fayoum, Egypt. He is one of the victims of the deterioration of Lake Qarun, having worked as a fisherman for 20 years alongside his father. The fish stocks in the lake have sharply declined due to severe pollution. Despite this, he has chosen to settle between Aswan and Fayoum, as he is unwilling to leave his land and roots. This displacement has resulted in the loss of ancestral roots and a deep emotional connection to the land Photograph: Fatma Fahmy/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen ‘The sardine, the only fish remaining is just like us. It searches for a place to rest, but the sea refuses to embrace it. Both of us are adrift and lost.’ Fatma Fahmy’s When Absence Takes Hold explores how the environmental degradation of Lake Qarun in Egypt has reshaped women’s relationships with family, body, memory, and place Photograph: Fatma Fahmy/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen A radioactivity testing laboratory in the Chornobyl exclusion zone. Through portraiture and documentary photography, The Invisible Force looks at how the rapid expansion of Richland, displacement of the Yakama Nation and decades-long environmental degradation challenge the town’s pervasive pro-nuclear narrative Photograph: Caroline Gutman/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Braden Sims and Jack Kirkham, members of the Richland high school Bombers football team, pose for a portrait after practice Photograph: Caroline Gutman/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen Caroline Gutman’s project, The Invisible Force, resonated with jurors ‘for its thoughtful approach on a subject wedged between the past and present’. They said: ‘Her focus and eye for detail shine a light on our collective histories and global war-making, asking us to consider the long-term impact of nuclear ambitions in the US and abroad – at a moment when global conflicts have reached their highest levels since World War II’ Photograph: Caroline Gutman/womenphotograph.com Share 
View image in fullscreen ‘My husband and children died. Only my son Mohamed remains, working in Aswan, while I work to keep our home standing. Before my husband’s death, I felt like a queen in my own house.’ Judges were struck by When Absence Takes Hold, Fatma Fahmy’s ecofeminist look at how Lake Qarun’s slow ecological collapse is playing out in the bodies and daily lives of the women who depend on it.
